questions.question: A person walks 5 km to a destination in 1 hour. On the return journey, they walk the same 5 km back to the starting point in 30 minutes. What is the average speed of the person for the entire journey?
questions.questionHtml: A person walks 5 km to a destination in 1 hour. On the return journey, they walk the same 5 km back to the starting point in 30 minutes. What is the average speed of the person for the entire journey?
questions.solution:
- Total distance = 5 + 5 = 10 km.

- Total time = 1 hour + 0.5 hour = 1.5 hours.

- Average speed = 10 / 1.5 = 6.67 km/h.

questions.questionHtml: A thief and a police officer are 500 meters apart. If they run in the same direction, the police officer catches the thief in 10 minutes. If they run towards each other, they meet in 2 minutes. What is the speed of the thief in meters per minute?
questions.solution:
- Same direction: (P - T) x 10 = 500 => P - T = 50.

- Opposite direction: (P + T) x 2 = 500 => P + T = 250.

- Solving: 2P = 300 => P = 150; T = 250 - 150 = 100 m/min.

questions.question: PASSAGE (Q.84-Q.88): Postcolonial infrastructures often inhabit a schizochronic condition—a simultaneity of obsolescence and futurity. Flyovers half-finished, railway stations calcified mid-renovation, and electric grids oscillating between blackout and surplus do not signify simple malfunction. Rather, they manifest a (1) ____ temporality in which the present is neither a continuity of the past nor a stable projection of the future. These infrastructures function not as inert utilities but as affective indexes of temporal rupture. Modernity, once telegraphed through asphalt and concrete, now flickers within these arrested developments—gestures of progress suspended in bureaucratic amber. Here, functionality is beside the point. What matters is the performative (2) ____ of development: roads that signify mobility even when impassable, metros that symbolise futurity even when immobile. In this schema, infrastructure ceases to be an engineering problem and becomes a narrative technology—a spatial discourse that (3) ____ the nation-state’s promises into sedimented form. Bridges-to-be and always-rebuilding airports constitute not failure, but continuity: the continual renewal of unfinished intention. Such spatial artefacts require a recalibrated hermeneutics. To read them literally is to miss their symbolic resonance. Their disrepair is not decay but (4) ____: a visual vocabulary of state temporality, in which incompletion is the political idiom of continuity. This is the temporal grammar of anticipation without arrival. Thus, the postcolonial built environment articulates not stasis, but (5) ____—a condition where motion exists without direction, and progress is simulated through perpetual incompletion. What should come in the place of blank number (1)? ...they manifest a (1) ____ temporality in which the present is neither a continuity of the past nor a stable projection of the future.
